skill_drafts.name: Collection Frequency vs Document Frequency Distinction
skill_drafts.description: Reference knowledge distinguishing collection frequency (cf) and document frequency (df) metrics in text retrieval. Use when selecting appropriate term weighting metrics for scoring or understanding why cf and df produce different ranking behaviors.
applicable_signals: Inconsistent ranking results when using cf vs df
Need to select term weighting metric for scoring function
Analyzing term importance across collection vs within documents
contraindications: Do not use when implementing actual tf-idf computation; use operational tf-idf procedures instead
Do not use for query expansion strategy selection
Do not use for tuning zone weights or parametric scoring
triggers: Choosing between collection-wide term frequency and document-specific term frequency for weighting
Debugging unexpected ranking differences between cf-based and df-based scoring
Evaluating why two terms with similar collection frequencies rank differently
constraints: This is reference-level knowledge, not an executable workflow
Provides metric distinction only; does not compute or apply weights
output_contract: Clear understanding that cf counts term occurrences across entire collection while df counts documents containing the term, leading to different weighting outcomes. Caller can then select appropriate metric for their scoring context.

examples.output: cf=10422 (total occurrences), df=8760 (documents containing it). High cf with high df indicates common term across many documents.
examples.notes: Suggests moderate discriminative power for ranking

examples.output: cf=10440 (total occurrences), df=3997 (documents containing it). Similar cf to 'try' but much lower df indicates concentrated occurrence.
examples.notes: Suggests higher discriminative power; term appears intensely in fewer documents

metadata.prompt: Collection frequency (cf) counts the total occurrences of a term across the entire collection. Document frequency (df) counts how many documents contain the term at least once. These metrics produce different weighting outcomes: a term with high cf but low df (e.g., appearing many times in few documents) signals different importance than a term with similar cf but high df (appearing across many documents). Use this distinction when choosing between collection-wide and document-specific term frequency for weighting schemes.
